odor: Odorless at ambient concentrations; slightly acidic taste
environmentalPersistence: Very high as atmospheric gas — atmospheric half-life ~100–300 years; absorbed by oceans and plants

lowDose.description: Enhanced photosynthesis (CO₂ fertilization effect) — increased growth, larger leaves, reduced stomatal aperture for equivalent CO₂ uptake (improved water use efficiency). Positive effect well documented in controlled conditions.

highDose.description: Excess CO₂ causes stomatal closure, reduced transpiration, impaired nutrient uptake via transpiration stream, and at extreme levels (>10,000 ppm) direct acidosis in mesophyll cells. Also reduces protein and nutrient concentration per unit biomass (dilution effect).

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Negative at low dose (promotes growth — CO₂ fertilization); mild at high dose via stomatal closure and nutrient dilution
morphologicalEffects.leafSize: Increased at low dose; slightly pale and larger at very high dose
morphologicalEffects.leafCurl: Minimal — not a primary CO₂ effect
morphologicalEffects.wilting: Minimal at low dose (improved WUE); mild at very high dose
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Absent at low dose; mild at high dose — nutrient dilution in rapidly grown tissue
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Only at extreme doses (>10,000 ppm) — acidosis in mesophyll
morphologicalEffects.pigmentation: Minimal — CO₂ does not induce anthocyanin
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Mildly stimulated at low dose (more carbohydrates for root growth); maintained
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: New growth benefits most at low dose; dilution chlorosis may appear on rapidly formed leaves at high dose

physiologyEffects.chlorophyllReduction: None at low dose; mild at high dose (nutrient dilution)
physiologyEffects.photosyntheticRate: Strongly increased at low dose; diminishing returns then mild decrease at very high dose
physiologyEffects.stomatalConductance: Decreased even at low dose — partial closure to maintain CO₂/H₂O tradeoff
physiologyEffects.transpiration: Reduced (improved WUE is key low-dose benefit)
physiologyEffects.waterUptake: Near-normal; mildly reduced at high dose via stomatal closure reducing transpiration pull
physiologyEffects.nutrientTransport: Mildly reduced at high dose — reduced transpiration stream reduces mass flow of nutrients

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: None at low dose; mild at very high dose
defenseProteins: minimal — CO₂ actually reduces jasmonate defense signaling (growth-defense tradeoff)

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Mild — elevated CO₂ alters root exudate composition and rhizosphere chemistry
microbiomeEffects.beneficialBacteriaEffect: Mixed — some PGPR benefit from increased root exudate carbohydrates; mycorrhizal associations may increase
microbiomeEffects.fungalEffect: Mycorrhizal colonization can increase under elevated CO₂ (more carbohydrate available for fungal partner)
microbiomeEffects.rhizosphereStability: Near-normal to mildly improved at low dose

firstSymptoms: increased growth and greening at low dose
lateSymptoms: dilution chlorosis and nutrient stress at high dose
temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: Immediate — stomata respond within minutes to CO₂ changes
temporalDynamics.sensitization: Acclimation reduces initial CO₂ fertilization benefit over time (photosynthetic downregulation)

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Low dose: taller, slightly paler green (dilution). High dose: pale green with stomatal surface matte appearance
visualSimulation.firstAffectedRegion: Stomatal surface — closure reduces visual shininess
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Near-normal appearance at low dose; important to show POSITIVE effect — largest plant in greenhouse should be CO₂-treated
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Green glow from enhanced sucrose and Calvin cycle activity — positive signal
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Immediate stomatal recovery; growth benefit persists

synergies.synergyNote: CO₂ fertilization effect is most pronounced when N is non-limiting — elevated CO₂ + adequate N produces maximum growth response. Without adequate N, CO₂ fertilization benefit is largely negated.
synergies.antagonismNote: CO₂ and ozone have opposing stomatal effects — CO₂ closes stomata reducing ozone uptake; but simultaneously ozone damage reduces CO₂ uptake for photosynthesis. Real-world climate scenario.

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, volcanic eruptions, respiration — current atmospheric concentration ~425 ppm (2024), up from 280 ppm pre-industrial
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: CO₂ enrichment used in commercial greenhouses (typically 1000–1500 ppm) to boost crop yields
educationalContext.humanToxicity: Not toxic at atmospheric concentrations; dangerous at high concentrations (>5000 ppm causes dizziness; >40,000 ppm lethal)
educationalContext.climateLink: THE primary anthropogenic greenhouse gas — the simulator should make clear that CO₂ is both a plant nutrient AND the primary driver of the climate crisis. The fertilization effect is real but insufficient to offset climate damage.
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Both — indoor elevated CO₂ common in crowded rooms; outdoor levels rising globally
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: CO₂ fertilization is real — climate change deniers use it to argue rising CO₂ is good for plants. But the full picture (heat stress, drought, ozone, etc.) negates the benefit. Teaches students to evaluate incomplete arguments.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Climate change, greenhouse horticulture, CO₂ fertilization vs climate damage tradeoff, food nutrition changes under elevated CO₂

sources: Long SP, et al. (2006). Food for thought: lower-than-expected crop yield stimulation with rising CO₂ concentrations. Science, 312(5782), 1918–1921.

Myers SS, et al. (2014). Increasing CO₂ threatens human nutrition. Nature, 510, 139–142.
